title: Migration 56 — batch dates become real dates in the right calendar
description: Applies migration 56 to the reconciled substrate, runs its VERIFY A-G, then rolls it back. Production stores harvest_date, cure_date, test_date and expiry_date as text, so the database cannot tell that '2026-13-45' is not a date, that a batch was tested three years before it was harvested, or that '2569-03-14' is a Thai Buddhist-Era year rather than a Common-Era one. The point that makes this migration more than a type change: converting to `date` does NOT catch the calendar error. PostgreSQL accepts DATE '2569-03-14' as a perfectly valid year-2569 date and stores it without complaint, which is why VERIFY C asserts that premise before asserting the refusal. What catches it is a bound on the YEAR -- a Buddhist-Era year for a real harvest is around 2560-2580 and a Common-Era one is around 2020-2030, and the ranges do not overlap this century. This deliberately does NOT store a BE year beside each date the way migration 40 does for permits: a permit is transcribed from a document that STATES a BE year, so storing both lets the database catch a transcription error, whereas a harvest date is a farm event and a second column would be inventing a field nobody wrote down. Requiring strict YYYY-MM-DD going in is what makes the rollback lossless: text -> date -> text round-trips exactly. NOT read-only; wrapped in BEGIN..ROLLBACK.

verify.note: C is the section that carries the migration. It first proves that PostgreSQL accepts a year-2569 date on its own -- so the reader knows the type is not the guard and the CHECK is doing real work -- and only then requires all four columns to refuse it. A bound written against a premise nobody checked is how this class of defect survives. D walks what the text column used to accept: an impossible day (2026-02-30), an impossible month (2026-13-01), free prose, and the empty string. F is the counterexample that stops the ordering rules being overstated -- a batch entered over two sittings has a test date and no harvest date yet, and refusing it would make this a constraint somebody removes; it also proves same-day harvest-cure-test is allowed, which is why the rule is >= and not >. G pins the bound at both ends in both directions: 2000 and 2100 admitted, 1999 and 2101 refused, so the range cannot be off by one. NOT PROVEN HERE: that a harvest date in the FUTURE is refused. A CHECK constraint must be IMMUTABLE so it cannot call current_date; catching that needs a trigger and a different migration. NOT PROVEN HERE either: that the application writes strict ISO -- the precondition refuses anything else at apply time, but the TypeScript layer is unchanged and still types these as strings.
